subtype: Following a grown-up's order to hurt [Actor]
passage: The Saturday music class at the community centre had one rule: Sir's word was final. Tanvir, ten, was row leader, which meant he stood at the end and passed out song sheets. Before the concert practice, Sir called him over. "Tell Damini to sit at the back and only listen today. She's off-key. Tell her clearly." Tanvir's hands went cold. Damini had practised the whole week; he had heard her humming at the gate. But Sir had taught music for thirty years. He must know. Tanvir walked over. "Sir says you sit at the back. You're off-key." Damini's mouth opened, then closed. She took her sheet and sat on the last bench, not singing. All through practice Tanvir kept thinking, Sir said it. Not me. His own voice sounded thin.

qa.q: What was Tanvir's job as row leader?
qa.a: He stood at the end and passed out song sheets.

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel when Sir gave him the order, and how did he calm himself?
qa.a: He felt uneasy, his hands going cold, but told himself Sir had taught music for thirty years and must know best.

qa.q: What could Tanvir have done instead of passing the message on?
qa.a: He could have told Sir that Damini had practised all week and asked Sir to speak to her himself, or kindly, instead of saying it harshly for him.

qa.q: How might Damini see Tanvir after he delivered the message?
qa.a: Damini may feel hurt and embarrassed, and see Tanvir as the one who shamed her, even though the words came from Sir.

grounding: A ten-year-old obeys a teacher's order to push a classmate out of singing, feeling uneasy but reasoning that the adult must know best.

passage: I'm Anjali. I study on the bench by our building's skating rink most evenings, so I saw this. Elizabeth, eight, is the coach's favourite, always first in line. On Tuesday a new girl came with old skates held together with tape. The coach skated over to Elizabeth and said something, pointing at the new girl. Elizabeth looked at the ground for a moment, then rolled over and said loudly, "Coach says you can't skate with our group. You'll slow us down." The new girl sat on the edge and unlaced her skates. Elizabeth kept looking back at her, falling more than usual. Later I heard her tell her mother, "Coach told me to. It's his rule." She said it twice, as if she needed to hear it.

qa.q: What held the new girl's old skates together?
qa.a: They were held together with tape.

qa.q: What does Elizabeth repeating 'Coach told me to' suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt uneasy and guilty, and was trying to push the responsibility onto the coach so she would feel better.

qa.q: What could Elizabeth's mother say when she hears this?
qa.a: She could gently ask how the new girl might have felt and help Elizabeth think of a way to include her next time, even if the coach said otherwise.

qa.q: What was the session like for the new girl?
qa.a: She was told by another child, in front of the group, that she could not join, and she spent the time on the edge unlacing her skates alone.

grounding: A child obeys a coach's instruction to exclude a new girl, and later insists it was the coach's rule, as seen by a neighbour.

passage: The scout camp was held in the school ground of a kasba outside Satara. Ganga, fifteen, was patrol leader, and the senior troop leader, Farhan, was a college boy everyone admired. When little Sonu came to assembly without his scarf, Farhan said calmly, "Ganga, make him stand in the sun. Just five minutes." Ganga did. Five minutes later: "Now arms out. Just continue." She hesitated. Sonu's lips were dry. "It's discipline. Continue," Farhan said, without raising his voice. Ganga's throat was tight, and her voice shook as she said, "Arms up, Sonu." Stopping now felt like saying the first five minutes were wrong. Then the scout teacher, Mrs Pillai, crossed the ground, stopped it at once, sat Sonu in the shade with water, and spoke to Farhan and Ganga separately before lunch.

qa.q: What did Sonu forget to bring to assembly?
qa.a: He came without his scarf.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling as she kept giving the orders?
qa.a: She felt tense and doubtful, her throat tight and her voice shaking, yet stopping felt harder because it would mean the first step had been wrong.

qa.q: At what point could Ganga have stopped, and how?
qa.a: At the first order she could have said calmly that making Sonu stand in the sun was not right, before each small step made stopping harder.

qa.q: How did it feel for Sonu to be punished by his own patrol leader?
qa.a: Sonu was left thirsty and exposed in the sun, obeying someone he trusted, with no one to ask for help until the teacher came.

grounding: A teenager told by an admired senior to punish a junior complies step by step while visibly distressed, because stopping feels harder than going on.

passage: The school newspaper office in Accra smelled of printer ink. Yara, sixteen, had just joined as a junior editor, and Nkechi, the senior editor, was someone she wanted to impress. "Review Kwesi's poem for Friday's issue," Nkechi said calmly. "Be honest. Start with the rhymes." Yara wrote that the rhymes were weak. Nkechi read over her shoulder. "Good. Now add a line about how it sounds like a birthday card." Yara typed it. Her stomach clenched. "And say readers deserve better. Just continue, you're doing fine." Yara's fingers hovered. Kwesi was in Form 2 and had shown her the poem in the corridor, shyly. But she had already written two lines; deleting them now felt like admitting she'd been wrong from the start. She typed the third sentence with her face burning, and felt, strangely, like she was watching someone else do it.

qa.q: What did Nkechi tell Yara to start with in the review?
qa.a: Nkechi told Yara to start with the rhymes.

qa.q: What was Yara feeling when her fingers hovered over the keyboard?
qa.a: She was torn and distressed, knowing Kwesi had shyly shown her the poem, but deleting the first lines felt like admitting she had been wrong.

qa.q: What could Yara still do before Friday's issue goes out?
qa.a: She could tell Nkechi she is not comfortable publishing a mocking review and rewrite it as fair, kind feedback, since the review is not printed yet.

qa.q: How might Kwesi feel if the review is published as it is?
qa.a: Kwesi would probably feel humiliated in front of the school, especially after trusting Yara enough to show the poem in the corridor.

grounding: A teenager guided calmly by a senior writes a harsher and harsher review of a junior's poem, distressed but finding it harder to stop than to continue.

passage:
Tuesday, library, 9 pm

Revising for the psych exam, I read the full account of that old obedience study. Ordinary men, told to give shocks to a stranger every time he got a word wrong. The stranger was an actor, but they didn't know. He yelled that his heart hurt. And a calm man in a grey coat said, "Please continue." Most of them did. All the way.

My first feeling: anger. How could they?

Then I read the notes on how they behaved. They sweated, argued, laughed nervously. They asked, "Is he all right?" None of them seemed cruel.

Walked back with Lokesh and told him. He asked, "Would you stop?" I said yes, fast. Then I remembered the canteen manager telling me to throw the leftover food in the drain instead of giving it to the boys at the gate, and I did it without a word.

I'm less sure now.
- Shankar

qa.q: What did the man in the grey coat say to the participants?
qa.a: He said, 'Please continue.'

qa.q: How did Shankar's feelings about the participants change as he read?
qa.a: Shankar's first feeling was anger at them, but after reading how they sweated, argued and asked if the man was all right, Shankar saw they were ordinary, not cruel.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Shankar, and what might he do with it?
qa.a: Remembering throwing the food away on the canteen manager's word showed Shankar that obeying without asking comes easily, so next time Shankar might pause and question such an order.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have seen Shankar's quick 'yes'?
qa.a: Lokesh may have suspected it was too easy an answer, which is why he asked the question in the first place.

grounding: A student reading about the obedience experiments moves from anger at the participants to seeing that the student could also be the one who complies.

passage: "You asked why I nearly quit the football academy, Rashmi. Here's the real reason. First month, the captain made a rule: we junior boys carry every senior's kit bag and are called 'Boot Boy' instead of our names. The seniors did it to us every evening, laughing. When I asked one of them, Ravi, why, he said, 'Captain's orders, Jeevan. If I don't, I'm on bags too.' That was the line from everyone: no choice. After three weeks I felt like a peg to hang bags on. I stopped using my own name in my head. Then one night I phoned my coach at home and told him everything. He came to the hostel that same night, said none of it was my fault, stopped the rule on the spot, and reported it to the academy director before morning."

qa.a: They were called 'Boot Boy' instead of their names.

passage: I'm Kavitha, and I shared a room with Shalini in our nursing hostel, so I saw this from close up. Our ward in-charge started a new policy: any trainee who made an error had her name read out at handover and was put on nights for a week. The staff nurses carried it out; they'd say, "Sorry, Shalini, orders," and then read her name like a charge sheet. Shalini, twenty-two, was on nights for three weeks straight. She stopped eating breakfast with us. Once I heard her say, "I'm just the mistake trainee," in a flat voice. I don't know everything she felt, but she looked at people as if she were furniture being moved. One evening I walked her to the principal's office. The principal listened to her for an hour, said the policy was not how anyone should be treated, and called the ward in-charge in that same evening.

qa.q: What happened to a trainee who made an error under the new policy?
qa.a: Her name was read out at handover and she was put on nights for a week.

qa.q: What does Shalini's flat 'I'm just the mistake trainee' suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she has started to see herself the way the policy treats her, as a label rather than a person.

qa.q: Which choice by Kavitha made a difference, and why?
qa.a: Walking Shalini to the principal's office brought the problem to someone with power, who listened, rejected the policy and called in the ward in-charge that evening.

qa.q: How did the staff nurses see their own part in the policy?
qa.a: They acted as if they had no choice, saying 'Sorry, Shalini, orders' before reading out her name.

grounding: A trainee targeted by a punitive policy carried out on a superior's orders feels treated as a thing, while those enforcing it insist they are only following orders.

passage:
Monday. Sangeeta, twenty-four, had been a lab chemist at the dye factory for five months when the shift manager said, "Tonight, flush the used dye tanks straight into the canal. The treatment unit is slow." Sangeeta felt the doubt at once. The canal ran past three villages. She said calmly, "Sir, I don't think that's safe. Could you give it to me in writing?" He waved her off. "Just do it."

Wednesday. She did not flush the tanks. She emailed the plant's safety officer asking for a second opinion and copied the manager, politely.

Friday. The manager called her in. "You're refusing?" "Yes, sir, unless the safety officer approves." Behind her, her colleague Gopika spoke up for the first time. "I'm not doing it either." The safety officer arrived that afternoon and ordered the treatment unit repaired.

qa.q: Where did the manager want the used dye flushed?
qa.a: He wanted it flushed straight into the canal.

qa.q: What was on Sangeeta's mind when the manager first gave the order?
qa.a: She felt immediate doubt, thinking of the three villages the canal ran past, and wanted the instruction on record before acting.

qa.q: Why was it important that Sangeeta objected on Monday rather than later?
qa.a: Raising the concern at the first doubt meant she never started the harmful act, so refusing stayed simple and gave Gopika the courage to join her.

qa.q: How might Gopika have felt when Sangeeta refused in front of the manager?
qa.a: Gopika probably felt relieved and braver, since one person's calm refusal made it easier to say no too.

grounding: A young chemist asked to do something harmful raises her doubt at once, asks for it in writing and a second opinion, declines, and helps a colleague refuse too.

passage: Sharmila, you asked what I did when I was new at the paper. Let me tell you. I was twenty-five, a junior reporter, and there had been a bus accident. My editor said, "Get the injured girl's photo from her family's shop and print her name with it. Readers want faces." She was fourteen. My stomach turned before I even left the room, and I thought, better say it now than after I've got the photo. So I went back in and said, quietly, "Sir, I don't think we should print a child's name and face. Could we check with the chief editor?" He was annoyed. "Put it in writing, then." I did, that evening. The chief editor agreed with me. The next morning another junior, Farah, told me she'd been asked the same and had been too scared to refuse. After me, she did. Your Mahima Masi was not a brave woman, beta. I just spoke up early.

qa.q: How old was the injured girl the editor wanted to photograph?
qa.a: She was fourteen.

qa.q: Why did Mahima go back to the editor straight away?
qa.a: Her stomach turned at once, and she felt it would be easier to object now than after she had already taken the photo.

qa.q: Which parts of Mahima's refusal made it both respectful and effective?
qa.a: She stated her concern calmly, suggested checking with the chief editor, and put it in writing, so the decision rested on more than one person's order.

qa.q: How did Mahima's refusal affect Farah?
qa.a: Farah, who had been too scared to refuse, found the courage to say no after seeing Mahima do it.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a young reporter, she questioned a harmful order early, asked for a second opinion in writing and declined, which helped a colleague refuse too.

subtype: Playing a role until it takes over [Actor]
passage:
Dear Ishita,

You asked what being bus prefect is like. I'll be honest, since you're my cousin and won't tell anyone. The little ones call me Prefect Didi.

In June the principal gave me a badge and a list of rules. I didn't know how to be strict, so I copied last year's prefect: arms folded, loud voice, "Sit down NOW." It felt like wearing someone else's jacket.

But it's November now and the jacket fits. Yesterday a Class 5 boy was singing, and I made him stand for the whole ride home. He's nine. I didn't even think about it. It was only when his little sister started crying at his stop that I heard myself, like a recording.

In June I would never have done that. Now it feels normal, and that's what scares me. I don't think I'm a mean person. I think I've been playing one so long I forgot.

Write back soon,
Aditi

qa.q: How long did Aditi make the Class 5 boy stand?
qa.a: She made him stand for the whole ride home.

qa.q: What scares Aditi when she thinks about the bus ride?
qa.a: She is scared that being harsh now feels normal, as if she has been playing a mean prefect so long she forgot it was an act.

qa.q: What turning point made Aditi notice the change, and what could she do next?
qa.a: The boy's little sister crying at his stop made her hear herself; she could apologise to the boy and drop the copied voice to find her own way of keeping order.

qa.q: How might the nine-year-old boy see Aditi now?
qa.a: He might see her as frightening and unfair, since he was punished for singing and had to stand in front of everyone the whole ride.

grounding: A teenage bus prefect who began by copying a tough manner finds the harshness has come to feel natural and changes what she thinks is acceptable.

passage: "Siddharth, you want to know why the juniors were scared of me last term? Okay. I got the role of the jail warden in our school play. Big boots, a fake moustache, a baton. Our drama teacher told us, 'Stay in character, even off stage, it helps.' So I did. At rehearsals I marched around and barked at the Class 8 kids who played prisoners. Everyone laughed; it was part of the fun. But after about three weeks I noticed I was barking at them in the canteen too, with no boots on. I made one of them give up his seat for me, and it felt completely normal. My mother said, 'Manoj, beta, why do you keep saying Silence at dinner?' After the final show I took off the moustache and still sounded like him. It took me a month to stop."

qa.a: Big boots, a fake moustache and a baton.

qa.q: What did Manoj feel when he made the junior give up his seat in the canteen?

qa.a: The teacher could have set a clear line that the character stays on stage, and checked in on how the junior actors were being treated off stage.

qa.q: How might the Class 8 juniors have experienced Manoj off stage?
qa.a: They probably felt scared and confused, since the barking no longer felt like a game once it followed them into the canteen.

grounding: A teenager cast as a harsh warden stays in character until the toughness spills into real life and starts to feel natural.

passage:
Wednesday night

Orientation committee, week two. We seniors run the 6 am roll call for first-years in the hostel courtyard. The warden set the time but left the rest to us. Committee T-shirts, whistles, a register.

Today Ritu was late for the third time. Four minutes. She said her alarm didn't ring. I took her phone for the night and made her read the hostel rules aloud to everyone. She stood there in her night suit with her voice cracking.

Honestly, she deserved it. These juniors think hostel is a holiday. Last year I was the one being shouted at and I learned.

When I gave the phone back just now, she said "Thank you, didi" very quietly, not looking at me. It bothered me for a second. Then I thought, that's respect. That's how it should be.

Nobody checks what we do in that courtyard. Maybe that's why it works.
- Kalyani

qa.q: How late was Ritu for the roll call today?
qa.a: She was four minutes late.

qa.q: What does Kalyani believe about Ritu and the other juniors?
qa.a: She believes they deserve harsh treatment because they think hostel is a holiday, and she takes Ritu's quiet thanks as respect.

qa.q: What went wrong in how the courtyard roll call was run, and what could fix it?
qa.a: With T-shirts, whistles and no one checking, the seniors punished at will; the warden could set clear limits and check the roll call personally.

qa.q: How might Ritu have felt reading the rules aloud with her voice cracking?
qa.a: Ritu likely felt humiliated and afraid, which explains why she thanked her senior quietly without looking at her.

grounding: A hostel senior on an orientation committee enforces rules harshly on a junior because the role allows it, and comes to believe the junior deserves it.

passage: Nandini, sit with your Farida Phuphi for a minute. You say you're only a trainee, so you keep quiet. I said the same thing once. At nineteen I joined a big tailoring house in Hyderabad as an apprentice. We were called 'the girls'. We swept, threaded needles, carried tea. The masters never asked what we thought. At first I carried a notebook of my own designs. By the fourth month I had stopped opening it. When a customer asked me about a sleeve, I said, 'Ask master-ji, I'm only the apprentice,' though I knew the answer better than he did. I went home angry every night, and I didn't even know at whom. The worst part was I started to believe I wasn't the kind of person who designs. It took a new master, years later, asking for my notebook, to remind me that the apprentice was a role, not me.

passage: The monsoon had grounded half the flights, and the airport terminal was packed with angry passengers. Maria, twenty, six weeks into her ground-staff traineeship, stood in her grey trainee vest while the blue-vest staff ran the counters. Trainees were not to speak on the microphone or answer rebooking questions; for six weeks she had been told, "Trainee, move the trolleys," "Trainee, stay back." A mother with a baby asked her which counter handled the Kochi flight. Maria knew. She had studied the board all morning. But she heard herself say, "Sorry, I'm only a trainee, please ask the desk." The mother turned away, tired. Simran, the other trainee, looked at her. "You knew that." Maria shrugged, jaw tight. "What's the point? They don't want us to think." She pushed the next trolley harder than she needed to.

qa.a: The trainees wore grey vests.

qa.q: Why did Maria say she was only a trainee even though she knew the answer?

qa.q: What could Maria do the next time she knows an answer?
qa.a: She could give the simple answer and point the passenger to the right counter, and ask her supervisor what trainees are allowed to help with.

qa.q: How might the mother with the baby have felt when Maria turned her away?
qa.a: The tired mother likely felt more frustrated and alone in the crowded terminal, since she did not get an answer the trainee could have given.

subtype: Seeing the role, not the person [Observer]
passage:
Note, 9 December. Written by Sangeeta, senior teacher, residential school.

Mohan, twenty-five, took over as boys' hostel warden this term. We have been friends since training college. At home he makes paper boats for his nieces and lets them win at ludo. Tonight I saw him make three Class 6 boys stand outside the dormitory in the cold for talking after lights-out. When one, Gopika's younger brother, started to cry, Mohan said, "Crying won't help you." That is not the Mohan I know.

I also know the job: sixty boys, no deputy, a principal who blames the warden for every complaint.

What I did next: I brought the boys inside, then waited until he was calmer. I said, "This isn't how you are at home. I think the job is pushing you somewhere you wouldn't go." He was silent, then asked if I'd help him draft fair rules and raise the need for a deputy with the principal.

qa.q: How many boys does Mohan look after as warden?
qa.a: He looks after sixty boys.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling when she saw Mohan with the boys outside the dormitory?
qa.a: Sangeeta was troubled and surprised, since the harsh warden in front of Sangeeta was not the gentle friend who plays ludo with his nieces.

qa.q: Which part of Sangeeta's approach helped Mohan listen?
qa.a: Waiting until he was calmer and linking his behaviour to the pressures of the job, rather than attacking him, let him admit it and ask for help.

qa.q: What was that cold night like for the three Class 6 boys?
qa.a: They were left outside in the cold and told crying would not help, which likely made them feel scared and unprotected by the person meant to care for them.

grounding: A teacher sees a friend become harsh in his warden role, notes it is not how he is at home, and raises it gently while recognising the job's pressures.

subtype: Seeing the role, not the person [Observer]
passage:
Friday night

Saw Deven at work today for the first time. He's a ticket checker on the metro now. A college boy didn't have a valid card, and Deven held him by the elbow in front of the whole platform and said, "People like you think rules are for others." The boy was shaking. Deven's voice was one I'd never heard.

This is the Deven who used to cry at the end of films. Who carries his grandmother's shopping bags without being asked.

My first thought was to message Jasleen, his sister, and say, "Your brother has become a bully." I didn't. I thought about his job: the fines targets, the cameras everywhere, the supervisors listening on radios.

Tonight I called him. I said, "Deven, today on the platform that wasn't you. At home you'd never talk like that. I think the uniform's doing something." Long pause. Then: "I didn't even notice."

- Alka

qa.q: What is Deven's job now?
qa.a: He is a ticket checker on the metro.

qa.q: Why did Alka decide not to message Jasleen?
qa.a: Alka realised blaming Deven would be unfair without thinking about the fines targets, cameras and supervisors that shape his job, and chose to speak to him directly.

qa.q: What did Alka do well when she called Deven?
qa.a: Alka named the behaviour plainly, reminded him of how he is at home, and linked it to the role, so he could hear it without feeling attacked.

qa.q: How might the college boy remember the moment on the platform?
qa.a: He would probably remember feeling shamed and frightened in public, as if he were a criminal rather than someone without a valid card.

grounding: A friend sees Deven turn harsh in his ticket-checker role, remarks it is not how he is at home, and raises it without hostility.

passage:
Tuesday, after shift

Three months as housekeeping supervisor at the hotel. Today I caught myself. Zubin had missed a corner under a bed in 412, and I was standing over him with the checklist, saying, "How many times do I have to tell you people?" He's twenty-two, sends half his pay home, and always holds the lift for guests.

I stopped mid-sentence and asked myself: would I talk to Zubin like this at the bus stop? No. Never.

So what's happening to me in that uniform?

Three things I did today:
1. Wrote the room-check rules on the staff board, so it's the rule, not my mood.
2. Asked the front-office manager to walk my floors with me once a week and tell me honestly what she sees.
3. At the evening huddle I said, "Tell me one thing I do that makes your work harder." Silence. Then Zubin said, "Standing over us, ma'am." Fair.

- Ritu

qa.q: Which room had Zubin missed a corner in?
qa.a: He missed a corner under a bed in room 412.

qa.q: What made Ritu stop mid-sentence?
qa.a: She suddenly asked herself whether she would speak to Zubin like that at the bus stop and knew she would never, which showed her the role was changing her.

qa.q: Which of Ritu's three steps protects most against the role taking over, and why?
qa.a: Writing the rules on the board and asking the front-office manager to walk her floors make things transparent and checked, so her mood no longer decides.

qa.q: How might Zubin have felt saying 'Standing over us' at the huddle?
qa.a: He was probably nervous but relieved to be asked, and it may have made him trust his supervisor more.

grounding: A young supervisor asks whether she would treat a worker this way outside work, then adds clear rules, outside oversight and a request for honest input.

passage:
Rekha: Charu, need to tell someone. I snapped at a resident today
Charu: at the hostel? what happened
Rekha: a girl came back 10 min after curfew. I made her wait outside the gate while I lectured her
Rekha: in the rain
Charu: oh Rekha
Rekha: I know. two months as warden and I'm turning into the warden we hated
Charu: what made you notice
Rekha: she said "sorry ma'am" like I was a jail guard. I thought, would I leave my own cousin outside in the rain? never
Charu: so what now
Rekha: apologised to her tonight. then wrote the late-return rules on the notice board so it's not about my mood
Rekha: asked the trust secretary to check the late register with me every month
Rekha: and I'm putting a suggestion box by the office. "what should the warden stop doing"
Charu: that's brave
Rekha: or scary. we'll see

qa.q: How late was the girl who came back after curfew?
qa.a: She came back ten minutes after curfew.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling when she heard the girl say 'sorry ma'am'?
qa.a: She felt shocked and ashamed, because she was being treated like a jail guard and realised she would never leave her own cousin outside in the rain.

qa.q: Which of Rekha's steps keeps the warden role in check, and why?
qa.a: Posting the rules, asking the trust secretary to review the late register monthly, and a suggestion box add transparency, oversight and honest input.

qa.q: How might the residents see the suggestion box by the office?
qa.a: They might be surprised at first but feel safer and more respected, knowing the warden wants to hear what should change.

grounding: A young warden pauses to ask whether she would treat someone this way outside work, apologises and sets up clear rules, oversight and honest input.
